# Context Window Architecture: the full contract

> Everything an AI agent needs to write a producer for, implement, or build an application on Context Window Architecture (CWA), a draft specification for assembling every model call from typed slots, in one file. It is generated from the website repository by npm run build:contract: llms.txt, spec §1 and the slots and authority values from the Spec page, the producer and assembler guides, every requirement from contract/requirements.json, and conformance/README.md. Where anything here disagrees with the Spec page, the Spec page holds.

## Orientation (llms.txt)

> Context Window Architecture (CWA) is a draft specification for assembling every model call from typed slots. Producers emit candidate items, the application authenticates them and freezes a snapshot, and an assembler turns that snapshot into a rendered payload and a trace, deterministically and without calling a model. It is a specification, not a library: three assemblers, in Python, TypeScript and Go, implement it, and none is released.

The model is four planes (governance, state, evidence, interaction), eleven slots and one item shape. Every item names one slot and one authority and carries its source, version and freshness. The assembler admits it or excludes it with a reason code, resolves the conflict groups the application declared, fits what is left to the token budget in tier order, and renders it in the order a versioned placement profile gives. The trace records every one of those decisions. Requirements are numbered R-1 onward; a number is permanent and never reused.

Which source holds: the Spec page is the normative text, and anything on another page that disagrees with it is wrong. Requirement text is authored in contract/requirements.json and JSON shapes in schema/, and conformance/README.md is normative wherever the requirements leave an ordering, tie-break, boundary or algorithm step open (R-21). Everything here is a draft: profiles carry `spec: "cwa/draft"`, every example profile is unevaluated, and nothing is released. The specification, schemas, cases and site are licensed Apache-2.0.

The specification defines three conformance claims, and no others (spec §1):

- A conformant producer emits items that meet section 2's rules for an item (R-1, R-2), reports each entry it suppresses (R-9), computes its scores and variants before assembly (R-18), and meets the rules for its kind. Its claim rests on its word.
- A conformant assembler meets every MUST an assembler can meet by itself, provides the four published tokenizers and renderers, and emits the trace R-21 lists. Its claim rests on a conformance report that passes every published case and rejects every published rejection.
- A conformant application, an agent loop included, uses a conformant assembler and only conformant producers, and meets the MUSTs only it can: it authenticates each producer, writes state, declares conflict groups, makes every read, retrieval and model call before it freezes the snapshot, enforces invariants and tool permissions outside the model, renders with a published renderer, and hands the payload to the model with each text in the role its renderer assigns and no text of its own. Its claim rests on its word, except for its assembler's part.

### Guides

- [Producers](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/llms-producers.txt): build a retriever, memory store, MCP adapter, state service, capability policy or other producer whose items an assembler admits
- [Assemblers](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/llms-assemblers.txt): call one of the three assemblers, or build one in a new language and prove it with the conformance cases
- [Full contract](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/llms-full.txt): this file, spec §1, the slots and authority values, both guides, every requirement and the conformance README, in one file
- [Implementation guide for coding agents](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/cwa.md): what an application integrating CWA does, one rule per line

### Applications and agents

- [Getting started](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/start.html): six steps from the prompt you send today to a snapshot an assembler renders, with a prompt-to-slots migrator
- [Integration sketch](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/assembly-sketch.txt): the application's side, which runs the producers and freezes the snapshot, and an outline of what the assembler then does
- [Payload template](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/payload.txt): the policy-first-chat/v1 profile's slots as cwa-messages/v1 renders them
- [Example snapshot](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/examples/messages-snapshot.json): a support-chat snapshot, with [the cwa-messages/v1 payload](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/examples/messages-payload.json) all three assemblers render from it, byte for byte
- [Agent frameworks](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/index.html#harness): where the assembler goes in the OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, the Claude Agent SDK, the Vercel AI SDK or a loop of your own, and when to skip CWA

### Specification

- [Spec](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/spec.html): the normative text: conformance, planes, slots and items, governance, admission and fitting, placement profiles, the trace, and the changelog
- [SPEC.md](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/SPEC.md): every numbered requirement as Markdown
- [contract/requirements.json](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/requirements.json): requirement IDs and text, the source SPEC.md and the Spec page are generated from
- [contract/reasons.json](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/reasons.json): every exclusion and refusal code, in the order a trace ranks them (R-21)
- [contract/slot-defaults.json](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/slot-defaults.json): each slot's plane, default authority, tier and policy fields (R-3)
- [contract/assembler-scope.json](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/assembler-scope.json): which part of each requirement an assembler can check, and which belongs to producers or the application

### Schemas

- [context_item](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/context_item.schema.json): one candidate item
- [producer_batch](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/producer_batch.schema.json): what a producer hands over, `{ items, excluded }`
- [snapshot](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/snapshot.schema.json): the frozen input to one assembly
- [trace](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/trace.schema.json): what every assembly emits, refused or not
- [profile](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/profile.schema.json): a versioned placement profile
- [route_policy](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/route_policy.schema.json): producers, slot rules, fitting order and fact precedence for one route
- [conflict_group](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/conflict_group.schema.json): a conflict the application declares
- [registry_lock](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/registry_lock.schema.json): profiles and route policies pinned by digest
- [conformance_report](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/conformance_report.schema.json): an implementation's run of the published cases

### Conformance

- [conformance/README.md](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/conformance/README.md): how to run a case, and the algorithm: trace order, timestamps, numbers, ordering, the snapshot digest, refusals, conflicts, supersession, deduplication, source diversity, fitting, snapshot checks, tokenizers and renderers, registry and reporting
- [Cases](https://github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/website/tree/main/conformance/cases): one directory per case, holding a snapshot, the expected trace and, unless the case expects a refusal, the expected payload bytes
- [Rejections](https://github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/website/tree/main/conformance/rejections): snapshots that each break one snapshot check, which an assembler rejects before assembly
- [Assembler page](https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/assembler.html): each implementation's imported report, and a matrix of every requirement's scope and status

## Conformance (spec §1)

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY are used as in RFC 2119. MUST is required for conformance; SHOULD is expected unless a reason is recorded; MAY is optional.

A conformant assembler meets every MUST an assembler can meet by itself, provides every tokenizer and renderer that Tokenizers and renderers in conformance/README.md requires, and can emit its trace as JSON with the fields R-21 lists. A conformant producer emits only items that meet section 2's rules for an item (R-1, R-2), which admission checks, plus the MUSTs aimed at producers: every producer reports each entry it suppresses (R-9) and computes its scores and variants before assembly (R-18), and, by kind, R-9 and R-14 bind memory, R-10 anything carrying user-controlled or fetched content, R-13 retrievers, R-15 MCP adapters, and R-18's variant rules anything that supplies variants. A conformant application uses a conformant assembler and only conformant producers, and meets the MUSTs no component can meet for it: it enforces invariants, tool permissions among them, outside the model (R-5, R-15), writes state (R-8), declares conflict groups (R-11), authenticates each producer and binds its identity outside the items (R-15), makes every external read, retrieval and model call before it freezes the snapshot, and freezes a new one for any retry (R-12, R-23), sets parser: true on every route whose response a downstream parser consumes (R-4), sets budget.input to the model's context limit less budget.reserved_output (R-16), versions its profiles (R-20) and deploys only evaluated ones (R-19). It renders with a renderer the published cases cover. It declares a tokenizer that reads nothing but the text it counts (R-23) and counts the model's tokens, or estimates them with a budget.margin_percent that covers the error for the route's text (R-16); the tokenizer may be its own, under an ID no published tokenizer uses. It hands the payload to the model with each text in the platform role its renderer assigns, text assigned none in a single user message, where the query alone is the live turn, and no text of its own. The roles R-7 has the assembler assign, and the count R-16 has it make, hold for the payload it renders, as its report shows; only this handoff makes them hold for what the model receives. The Assembler page marks each requirement as assembler, boundary or application, so you can see who owns which part.

These are the only claims this specification defines. An application is not conformant because one of its parts is, though it may say which of its parts are. The claims also differ in kind. Producer and application conformance is an agreement about what each emits and does. Assembly cannot confirm all of it, so the claim rests on their word, and an assembler's boundary checks catch only some breaches. An assembler's conformance concerns what it decides. A wrong decision fails silently, because a model accepts any payload, so the claim rests on evidence: a conformance report showing that the assembler passes every published case and rejects every published rejection, skipping only those that use an optional tokenizer or renderer it does not provide, as Reporting results in conformance/README.md describes. An application's claim includes its assembler's, which is why it must render with a renderer the published cases cover: that assembler's report then backs how the payload is built. Its tokenizer need not be one the cases cover: they test how an assembler applies a tokenizer's counts, and no case can test whether those counts match a model only the application calls. That, and the handoff to the model, rest on the application's word like the rest of its claim.

Requirements are numbered R-n in a single flat sequence. A number is assigned once and never reused. A withdrawn requirement keeps its number and is marked withdrawn in the index. Other pages on this site, and the reference implementation, cite requirements by number.

The published JSON Schemas define item and trace field shapes. Profiles place slots and pick their wrappers, a published renderer writes the request from them, and wire encodings must preserve these semantics. The website tools check structure and selected local invariants, not full implementation conformance.

## Planes, slots and authority values (spec §2 and §3.1)

A model call is assembled from items. Every item belongs to exactly one slot, and slots are grouped into four planes, which answer four different questions and are never merged. Each slot takes the authority its defaults name (R-1); the producer guide below has the full table of defaults.

### Governance: Who may direct the model

- `governance.instructions`: Identity, goals, refusals, and safety boundaries: the system's constitution. This slot is never omitted and admits only governing-authority items. Items that aren't verified, or that carry the injection marker, are excluded here.
- `governance.capabilities`: The tools, functions and resources the model is permitted to invoke, with their contracts. Only tools the route's capability policy allows for this user are admitted, against a versioned allow-list. Permission is decided outside the model.
- `governance.examples`: Developer-owned input/output pairs that steer reasoning, tone or format, ranked by task similarity. A route that wants them places the slot and lists a producer for it; admission applies the same four slot rules as anywhere else (R-3). They defer to instructions and the output contract. They're droppable, so under budget pressure they go before anything compressible.
- `governance.output_contract`: Structure, style, length and schema of the response about to be generated. The contract is never omitted when a downstream parser exists. If a safety disclosure has to appear, make room for it in the contract itself. Conflict resolution can't drop a protected item, so a clash between the two escalates.

### State: What is true right now

- `state.user`: Durable profile, entitlements, locale, permissions, session preferences, each a separate item with its own freshness. Items are scoped to the current tenant and user. Unverified user claims remain source-linked memory; only application-confirmed facts enter state.
- `state.task`: Workflow stage, approval status, selected entity IDs, pending action, retry count. Task state is written by the application's state machine and never inferred from conversation.

### Evidence: What the model may ground on

- `evidence.knowledge`: Retrieved chunks, each sent as its own evidence item with source, version, relevance and trust. Each one has to clear admission: a relevance score at or above the route's min_relevance, and inside its freshness limits. Where the route asks for it, exact duplicates go after conflicts are resolved (R-24). An empty result is recorded as an outcome, not treated as an error.
- `evidence.tool_results`: Observations returned by tools already called, possibly several per loop, and any retrieved chunks a route sends here. When the route sets supersede: source, the newest observation from each producer and source stays and the older ones go (R-25). That's keyed on source, not on the tool call. An observation is evidence, not permission to act.

### Interaction: What has happened, and what is asked

- `interaction.memory`: Condensed summaries of older turns and inferred long-term facts, each linked to the turn it came from. Every entry carries an expires deadline and a source naming the turn it came from. Entries whose expires is at or before assembly_time, or that carry revoked_by, are excluded and show up in the trace (R-9). The assembler doesn't decide what's been contradicted; the application revokes it.
- `interaction.history`: A verbatim transcript of the most recent turns, bounded by turn count and tokens. Before assembly, overflow gets summarised into memory rather than cut mid-thought. Under budget pressure, when the route declares no fitting order, turns with a shorter variant switch to it first; after that, whole turns are dropped, oldest first unless the turns carry relevance scores or the route ranks the slot differently. Prior model turns carry lineage: generated and untrusted authority, and every prior turn renders inside the history transcript, never as a platform message. Turns render in the order they were said: by freshness, then id (R-7).
- `interaction.query`: The most recent, unprocessed input the model must respond to. The query is never omitted and always carries user authority. It is the trigger for generation, placed wherever the route's profile puts it.

### Authority values

| Authority | Role | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `governing` | Governing instruction | System and developer policy, safety constraints, the output contract, admitted capabilities, and steering examples. |
| `user` | User intent / preference | What the user asks for and how they want it. It cannot lift a constraint set above it. |
| `state` | Canonical state | Application-owned facts about the task and session. The route defines the facts for which this source is canonical. |
| `reference_only` | Reference evidence | Retrieved chunks in knowledge, which inform the answer but never direct behaviour. |
| `observation` | Tool observation | What a tool returned, and any retrieved chunk a route sends to tool results: evidence about the world, not permission to act on it. |
| `generated` | Generated memory | Summaries and inferences the system wrote. They are fallible, they expire, and they can be revoked. |
| `untrusted` | Untrusted (least privilege) | Prior model turns in history, which must carry it, and any other item in tool results, memory or history whose producer wants it handled with the least privilege. It keeps the item out of an instruction group's peers and changes nothing else. Governance, knowledge, state and the query never carry it. Not the same as injection_risk: untrusted_content, which flags content that might carry an injection. |

## Producers (llms-producers.txt)

> How to build a producer for Context Window Architecture (CWA): anything that emits candidate items into a slot, such as a retriever, a memory store, an MCP adapter, a state service, the capability policy, a policy loader or the conversation. It follows the Producers page, https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/producers.html. Rules are cited by their permanent number (R-n) and are normative on the Spec page, https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/spec.html. Its list of stages, its tables of slots, authority values and exclusion codes, and its example batch are generated from the contract by the website build.

### What a producer is

The assembler does not know how a producer works. It knows only what the producer hands over, and that handover is the contract. The application authenticates each producer and the route policy lists it under that identity, with one of seven kinds and the slots it may send: `retrieval`, `memory`, `mcp`, `state`, `capability_policy`, `policy` or `interaction` (R-15). Nothing in an item's own fields proves who sent it, neither `source` nor `trust`.

A conformant producer (spec §1) emits only items that meet section 2's rules for an item (R-1, R-2), which admission checks, plus the MUSTs aimed at producers:

- every producer reports each entry it suppresses (R-9) and computes its scores and variants before assembly (R-18);
- by kind, R-9 and R-14 bind memory, R-10 anything carrying user-controlled or fetched content, R-13 retrievers, R-15 MCP adapters, and R-18's variant rules anything that supplies variants.

The claim rests on the producer's word. Admission catches some breaches and excludes the item with a reason code the trace records; others, such as a retriever that merged chunks or dropped one without reporting it, no assembler can see.

### Who owns which stage

Between a source and the payload there are eight steps (spec §4). The first four are the producer's and happen before assembly starts. The last four are the assembler's, and everything it leaves out shows up in the trace with a reason code.

1. Rewrite (producer): Decide whether to rewrite the query for retrieval, and keep the rewritten form so you can explain the results later.
2. Retrieve (producer): Pull candidate chunks from sources whose provenance you can name.
3. Rerank (producer): Score each candidate against the query and put the score in relevance. If you drop a near-duplicate, report it as duplicate_content, with duplicate_of naming the one you kept (R-13).
4. Package (producer): Send each chunk as its own evidence item with source, source_version, relevance and the authority its evidence slot takes (R-1). Never one merged blob (R-13).
5. Admit (assembler): Check each item against its schema and the route: who sent it, which slot, what authority, its scope, age and expiry, and the route's min_relevance. Anything that fails is excluded with a reason code.
6. Resolve (assembler): Settle the conflict groups the application declared (R-11). Then, in the slots where the route asks, drop superseded observations (R-25), exact duplicates (R-24) and anything past max_per_source (R-26), in that order.
7. Fit (assembler): Refuse before any reduction if protected content can't fit (R-16, R-17). Otherwise apply item and slot caps, then shed in tier order under budget pressure: droppable first, then compressible (R-16). If too little evidence is left on a route that requires it, refuse instead (R-12).
8. Render & trace (assembler): Render the payload in the profile's order, hash it, and write a trace that accounts for every decision above (R-21).

### The batch

Whatever its kind, a producer hands over one batch per call: `{ items, excluded }`, as schema/producer_batch.schema.json defines it. When the application freezes the snapshot it adds `producer: { id, kind }`, the identity it authenticated for the batch, never read from item fields (R-15).

- `items` are your candidate items, each admitted or excluded on its own. An entry that is not a JSON object is not an item: the snapshot holding it is rejected (R-2, R-17).
- `excluded` has one row per entry you suppressed: `{ item_id, reason, stage: "producer" }`, with `reason` one of the exclusion codes below (R-9). A `duplicate_content` row carries `duplicate_of` and a `superseded` row `superseded_by`, no other row carries either, and each names a candidate in the same batch (R-9, R-13).
- Ids are unique across `items` and `excluded`, and across the snapshot: a candidate whose id another candidate or a producer exclusion uses, in any batch, is excluded with `duplicate_item_id` (R-2).
- A snapshot holds at most one batch per producer (R-15). A second batch from the same producer, an excluded row whose `duplicate_of` or `superseded_by` names no candidate in its batch, or a `reason` that is not an exclusion code rejects the whole snapshot before assembly, with no payload and no trace (R-17).
- Your rows reach the trace as reported, at `stage: "producer"` and with no slot, ahead of the assembler's rows, even from a batch whose producer the route does not admit (R-9). Every other row is the assembler's own, at `stage: "assembler"`.

The published example batch, examples/producer-batch.json:

```json
{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "refunds-eu:v17#p4",
      "slot": "evidence.knowledge",
      "source": "policy-corpus",
      "source_version": "2026-09-10",
      "authority": "reference_only",
      "trust": "verified",
      "freshness": "2026-09-12T15:30:00Z",
      "expires": "2026-12-12T15:30:00Z",
      "scope": {
        "tenant": "acme",
        "task": "refund_request"
      },
      "relevance": 0.91,
      "token_budget": 420,
      "tier": "compressible",
      "variants": [],
      "conflict_policy": "defers",
      "injection_risk": "untrusted_content",
      "lineage": "verbatim",
      "eligibility": "support-chat/illustrative/v1: tenant acme; rerank at least 0.5",
      "body": "Pro plans refund in full within 30 days of purchase."
    }
  ],
  "excluded": [
    {
      "item_id": "memory:expired",
      "reason": "expired",
      "stage": "producer"
    }
  ]
}
```

### The item

Every item carries eight fields: `id`, `slot`, `source`, `source_version`, `authority`, `freshness`, `trust` and `body`. Without them the assembler cannot place, rank, expire or trace the item, so it excludes it with `missing_field:<name>` (R-2). Two slots need one more, whoever produces the item: every `interaction.memory` item carries `expires` (R-9), and every `evidence.knowledge` item its rerank score in `relevance` (R-13). The item schema is closed, so an undeclared field, a wrong type or a malformed timestamp is `invalid_structure`.

| Field | Required | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | always | A string with at least one character that is not whitespace, unique in the snapshot. An item without one is recorded as `{producer id}#invalid-{n}` (R-2). |
| `slot` | always | One of the eleven slots in the table below; any other value is `unknown_slot` (R-1). |
| `source` | always | What the item came from: a document, turn, tool call, database field or memory write. A retriever sets it to the document a chunk comes from, so chunks of one document share it (R-26); repeated reads of the same thing share one, so supersession can keep the latest (R-25); a memory item names the turn it came from (R-9). |
| `source_version` | always | The version of that source. The trace repeats it for every included occurrence (R-22). |
| `authority` | always | One of seven values, fixed by the slot (R-1); see the tables below. |
| `freshness` | always | When the content was observed or true, an RFC 3339 date-time. It is not an expiry. |
| `trust` | always | `verified`, `unverified` or `untrusted`: the producer's own claim about its source, so it proves nothing (R-15). Only the governance gate reads it: a governance item must be `verified` (R-10). It never decides who may instruct or which fact wins. |
| `body` | always | The content. Assembly renders a body whole and never splits, edits or truncates it. |
| `expires` | memory | An absolute deadline, not a duration. Any item, memory or not, whose `expires` is at or before `assembly_time` is excluded as `expired` (R-9). |
| `relevance` | knowledge | The rerank score, a finite number, read as an IEEE 754 double like every number in a snapshot (R-2). A score equal to the slot's `min_relevance` passes (R-13). |
| `scope` | no | Any of `tenant`, `user`, `session`, `task`, `locale` and `step`. Every key you set must equal the request's value for it, and a slot's `required_scope` lists keys you must set; a missing key is never a wildcard (R-2). |
| `tier` | no | `protected`, `compressible` or `droppable`. Leave it out to take the slot's tier. You may lower it, except in a slot protected by default, and never raise it (R-16). |
| `revoked_by` | no | Set when the application revoked the item. Any item carrying it is excluded as `revoked` (R-9). |

Six policy fields describe how an item may be handled. A producer that knows better than the slot default SHOULD set them; when it does not, the assembler fills them from the slot defaults, or from the route's versioned overrides, and the trace lists every field it filled in `defaults_filled` (R-3).

- `token_budget` caps the tokens of the item's rendered body. `null`, the default, sets no cap of its own; the payload budget and the slot's `max_tokens` still bound the item. An item over its cap is reduced whether or not the payload fits: a compressible item to a variant within the cap, or else it is omitted, and a droppable item is omitted. A protected item over its cap is never cut: the assembly refuses with `protected_content_over_budget` (R-16).
- `variants` holds shorter bodies you computed ahead of time (see Variants and scores below). It defaults to an empty list.
- `conflict_policy` is `defers`, `governs` or `escalate`. It matters only inside a conflict group the application declares, and only between the peers that may instruct: the members at the highest instructing authority present. When exactly one peer governs and the rest defer, the deferring ones are excluded with `conflict_deferred`; any other pattern escalates (R-11). Facts ignore it; route policy decides them.
- `lineage` is `verbatim`, `summarised`, `redacted`, `translated`, `extracted` or `generated`.
- `eligibility` is a short description of why the item belongs in the request, for whoever reads the trace. It is never code and never blank, and the trace repeats it for every included occurrence (R-3, R-22). The route's slot rules decide what is eligible: `min_relevance`, `max_age_seconds`, `required_scope` and `source_prefix`, and no others (R-3).
- `injection_risk` is `none` or `untrusted_content` (see Untrusted content below).

Every date-time is `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS`, an optional fraction of any length, then `Z` or an offset `±HH:MM`. The date must exist, there are no leap seconds, and assemblers compare instants at their full stated precision (R-2). An item whose `freshness` is later than `assembly_time` by more than the route's `clock_skew_seconds` (default 0) is excluded with `future_freshness`.

### Slots, authority and defaults

Each slot takes the authority shown, and the defaults fill the policy fields an item omits (R-1, R-3; contract/slot-defaults.json):

| Slot | Plane | Holds | Authority | Tier | Lineage | injection_risk | conflict_policy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `governance.instructions` | Governance | Identity, goals, refusals, and safety boundaries: the system's constitution. | `governing` | protected | verbatim | none | governs |
| `governance.capabilities` | Governance | The tools, functions and resources the model is permitted to invoke, with their contracts. | `governing` | protected | verbatim | none | governs |
| `governance.examples` | Governance | Developer-owned input/output pairs that steer reasoning, tone or format, ranked by task similarity. | `governing` | droppable | verbatim | none | defers |
| `governance.output_contract` | Governance | Structure, style, length and schema of the response about to be generated. | `governing` | protected | verbatim | none | governs |
| `state.user` | State | Durable profile, entitlements, locale, permissions, session preferences, each a separate item with its own freshness. | `state` | droppable | extracted | none | governs |
| `state.task` | State | Workflow stage, approval status, selected entity IDs, pending action, retry count. | `state` | protected | extracted | none | governs |
| `evidence.knowledge` | Evidence | Retrieved chunks, each sent as its own evidence item with source, version, relevance and trust. | `reference_only` | compressible | verbatim | untrusted_content | defers |
| `evidence.tool_results` | Evidence | Observations returned by tools already called, possibly several per loop, and any retrieved chunks a route sends here. | `observation` | compressible | verbatim | untrusted_content | governs |
| `interaction.memory` | Interaction | Condensed summaries of older turns and inferred long-term facts, each linked to the turn it came from. | `generated` | compressible | summarised | untrusted_content | defers |
| `interaction.history` | Interaction | A verbatim transcript of the most recent turns, bounded by turn count and tokens. | `user` | compressible | verbatim | untrusted_content | defers |
| `interaction.query` | Interaction | The most recent, unprocessed input the model must respond to. | `user` | protected | verbatim | untrusted_content | defers |

The authority column has two exceptions: a prior model turn in `interaction.history`, marked `lineage: generated`, carries `untrusted`, and any other item in `evidence.tool_results`, `interaction.memory` or `interaction.history` may carry `untrusted` instead (R-1). An authority outside the seven is `unknown_authority`, and one the slot does not take is `authority_not_allowed`. Only `governing` and `user` items may instruct the model; the other five values record where data came from and are not a ranking of which facts are true (R-6).

| Authority | Role | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `governing` | Governing instruction | System and developer policy, safety constraints, the output contract, admitted capabilities, and steering examples. |
| `user` | User intent / preference | What the user asks for and how they want it. It cannot lift a constraint set above it. |
| `state` | Canonical state | Application-owned facts about the task and session. The route defines the facts for which this source is canonical. |
| `reference_only` | Reference evidence | Retrieved chunks in knowledge, which inform the answer but never direct behaviour. |
| `observation` | Tool observation | What a tool returned, and any retrieved chunk a route sends to tool results: evidence about the world, not permission to act on it. |
| `generated` | Generated memory | Summaries and inferences the system wrote. They are fallible, they expire, and they can be revoked. |
| `untrusted` | Untrusted (least privilege) | Prior model turns in history, which must carry it, and any other item in tool results, memory or history whose producer wants it handled with the least privilege. It keeps the item out of an instruction group's peers and changes nothing else. Governance, knowledge, state and the query never carry it. Not the same as injection_risk: untrusted_content, which flags content that might carry an injection. |

The tier column is the highest tier your items can claim. Only the route's versioned policy can raise a slot's tier, and an item that claims more than its slot's tier is excluded with `tier_upgrade_not_allowed`, so a producer cannot protect its own items. In a slot that is protected by default the tier is also the lowest: an item that sets a lower one there is excluded with `protected_tier_changed`. Anywhere else you may lower an item's tier, say to `droppable` so it sheds earlier, even in a slot only the route raised to protected (R-16).

### Producer kinds

A producer's kind limits the slots it may send, whatever the route lists, and an item in a slot the route does not list for its producer is excluded with `producer_slot_not_allowed` (R-15). An item from a producer the route does not list, or lists with another kind, is excluded with `producer_not_authenticated`.

#### Retrieval: evidence.knowledge and evidence.tool_results

One scored item per chunk, never a blob (R-13). Emit one evidence item per chunk, with `authority: reference_only` in knowledge or `observation` in tool results, its rerank score in `relevance` and its `source_version`, and set `source` to the document the chunk comes from, so chunks from one document share it. The retriever owns rewrite, retrieve, rerank and package, and any near-duplicate filtering: report each chunk it drops as a near-duplicate in `excluded` with reason `duplicate_content` and `duplicate_of` naming the chunk it kept, a candidate in the same batch. Every `evidence.knowledge` item, from any producer, carries `relevance`, or it is excluded with `missing_field:relevance`. An item a retriever sends to any slot but the two evidence slots is excluded with `producer_slot_not_allowed`, whatever the route lists.

An empty result set is a valid, recorded outcome, so do not pad it: on a route that requires evidence, the assembler refuses with `evidence_required` and a recovery action, and any retry is a new snapshot (R-12). Nor over-fill it: send no more chunks than the route's budget can use, since every chunk the assembler sheds for budget costs a count of the whole payload.

#### Memory: interaction.memory

The state-versus-memory distinction, expressed as fields (R-9, R-14). Emit only `generated` or `untrusted` items. Every entry carries `expires`, an absolute deadline, not a duration. Its `source` identifies the turn it was derived from; a route may set the slot's `source_prefix`, such as `turn:`, and an entry whose source lacks it is excluded with `source_invalid` (R-3). Omit `lineage` and the slot default, `summarised`, is filled in.

The producer does not decide what the user has contradicted: the application revokes the entry, and the store records `revoked_by`. Never emit an expired or revoked entry as a candidate. Report each in the batch's `excluded` list with reason `expired` or `revoked` and `stage: "producer"`, without its body, and the assembler merges those rows into its trace. An item sent to any slot but `interaction.memory` is excluded with `producer_slot_not_allowed`, whatever the route lists.

#### State: state.user and state.task

Owned by the application, and either current or absent (R-8). A state producer reads the database or the workflow engine and emits one item per fact, typed, with `authority: state` and `freshness` set to the read time. It never derives a value from conversation, and claims the user made about themselves go to memory, not state. The route lists it with `kind: state`: a state item from any other kind of producer is excluded with `producer_slot_not_allowed`, whatever slots the route lists for it, and an item older than the slot's `max_age_seconds` is excluded as `stale_state`.

`state.task` is protected by default: it is never shed, an item that sets a lower tier there is excluded with `protected_tier_changed`, and a `state.task` item over its own `token_budget`, or `state.task` items over the slot's `max_tokens`, refuse the whole assembly with `protected_content_over_budget`. `state.user` is droppable by default, so it sheds first under budget pressure, and an item that claims a higher tier is excluded with `tier_upgrade_not_allowed` (R-16).

#### MCP: evidence.tool_results and evidence.knowledge

Results go to evidence; tool specifications are proposed, never placed (R-15). Tool results and resources become `evidence.tool_results` items with `authority: observation`, or `evidence.knowledge` items with `reference_only`, each with a `freshness` and `injection_risk: untrusted_content` unless the route lists the server with `verified: true`. That flag is the route's to grant, never the adapter's (R-10), and it does nothing else: it never ranks the server's claims in a fact group (R-11). A resource bound for knowledge needs a `relevance` score like any retrieved chunk. Where the route sets `supersede: source` on tool results, only the newest observation per source survives (R-25), so give repeated reads of the same thing the same `source`. A resource that contains imperatives is still evidence.

Tool specifications are proposed to the route's capability policy; the adapter never writes to `governance.capabilities` itself. An item it emits there is excluded with `capability_not_allowed` where the route lists that slot for the adapter, and with `producer_slot_not_allowed` otherwise, as is anything it sends to a slot other than the two evidence slots, whatever the route lists.

#### Capability policy: governance.capabilities

Owned by the application, and the only producer for this slot (R-15, R-5). The capability policy holds the versioned allow-list of tools per route and user. It takes proposed specifications from MCP adapters and local tool registries, admits the ones this user may use, and emits one item per tool with `authority: governing`, `trust: verified` and `injection_risk: none`. The allow-list makes a natural `source`, and its version with the specification's content hash a natural `source_version`.

The route lists the policy with `kind: capability_policy`, and the snapshot carries its grant, `capabilities: { policy_producer, allow_list_version, allowed_ids }`. A `governance.capabilities` item is admitted only when its batch comes from the grant's `policy_producer`, the route lists that producer with kind `capability_policy`, and `allowed_ids` names the item's id; any other is excluded with `capability_not_allowed`. Permission is decided here, outside the model: the model is told what it may call, and the tool guard still enforces it.

#### Policy and interaction: whatever the route lists

These two kinds have no slot rule of their own. They may send whatever slots the route lists for them, except the state slots, which take only kind `state` (R-8), and `governance.capabilities`, which takes only the capability policy's grant (R-15). In the published route policies, a `policy` producer sends the governance slots and an `interaction` producer, the conversation, sends `interaction.history` and `interaction.query`.

- Governance items carry `authority: governing`, `trust: verified` and `injection_risk: none`. One that is not verified, or is marked `untrusted_content`, is excluded with `untrusted_in_governance` (R-10).
- The query carries `user` authority, keeps it although it is marked `untrusted_content`, and is the only live user turn (R-1, R-7, R-10).
- Prior turns go to `interaction.history` and render as a transcript inside the profile's history wrapper, never as platform messages (R-7). A user turn carries `user`; a prior model turn carries `lineage: generated` and `authority: untrusted` (R-1).

### Untrusted content

Every item in an evidence slot, in memory, in history and in the query carries `injection_risk: untrusted_content`, whoever produced it: retrieved chunks, tool output, memory and user turns alike (R-10). The slot default fills it when you omit it, and an item that sets `none` there is excluded with `untrusted_content_unmarked`. The one exception is output from an MCP server the route lists with `verified: true`, which only the authenticated route policy can grant (R-15).

The marker never changes authority or where an item renders (R-6, R-10). Material a user pastes or attaches into the body of a query or history item renders with that body, since assembly never splits one, and gains no authority from it; delimit such material inside the body in a form it cannot imitate. Material you receive separately belongs in an item of its own, marked.

### Variants and scores

Compression variants and rerank scores are the producer's job, computed before assembly, and they should be cached by content hash. Assembly never calls a model (R-18). If your producer can offer a shorter form of an item, emit it as a variant on the item, not as a second item. Each variant is `{ id, body, method, lineage }`, with an id distinct from its parent's and its siblings' (or the item is excluded with `duplicate_variant_id`). It inherits the parent's provenance, scope and authority, and must not add an instruction or a fact the parent does not support.

The assembler picks a variant only when its rendered body is shorter than the item's current one. An item over its `token_budget` takes its longest variant within the cap, and a compressible item with none is omitted (R-16). Under budget pressure, droppable items go first, except those a slot held at its `min_tokens` floor keeps, and then compressible items are compressed or omitted in the route's fitting order, variants first when the route declares none. Protected items are never compressed, truncated or omitted. Every omission is traced as `over_budget`.

### Admission failures

Every exclusion lands in the trace as `excluded[] { item_id, reason, stage }`, plus `duplicate_of` or `superseded_by` when the reason calls for it. When an item fails several checks, the assembler records the earliest code in this list, and among several missing fields the alphabetically first (R-21). These are the codes a producer can meet, in that order (contract/reasons.json):

| Code | Rule | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `producer_not_authenticated` | R-15 | The route policy does not list this batch's producer, or lists it with a different kind. Identity comes from the application's authentication and the route, never from item fields. A snapshot with two batches from one producer is rejected before assembly. |
| `missing_field:<name>` | R-2 | A required field of the item itself is absent: one of the eight minimum fields, or a slot-specific one such as expires for memory or relevance for knowledge. A variant missing one of its fields is invalid_structure. Fix the producer; the assembler will not guess. |
| `unknown_slot` | R-1 | The slot name is not one of the eleven. Check spelling and plane prefix. |
| `unknown_authority` | R-1 | The authority value is not one of the seven roles. capability and steering are not authority values; use governing with a conflict_policy. |
| `invalid_structure` | R-2 | The item fails the published schema for another reason, such as a wrong type, an undeclared field or a malformed timestamp. |
| `duplicate_item_id` | R-2 | Another candidate, in any batch and whatever its own outcome, or a producer exclusion from any batch uses this ID. Each candidate sharing it is excluded with the earliest code that applies to it. |
| `producer_slot_not_allowed` | R-15 | The authenticated producer is not permitted to emit into this slot: the route does not list the slot for it, or its kind rules the slot out whatever the route lists. State slots take only kind state (R-8), a memory producer only interaction.memory (R-14), a retrieval producer only the evidence slots (R-13), and an mcp producer only the evidence slots, plus governance.capabilities when the route lists it for the producer, where capability_not_allowed applies (R-15). |
| `authority_not_allowed` | R-1 | The authority value is not allowed for this slot. Each slot takes its own role, a prior model turn in history takes untrusted, and only other items in tool results, memory and history may carry untrusted instead (R-1): never governance, knowledge, state or the query. These roles are not a factual ranking. |
| `capability_not_allowed` | R-15 | The snapshot carries no capability grant, the authenticated emitter is not the producer the grant names as policy_producer listed by the route with kind capability_policy, or the tool is not on the grant's allow-list. Item source strings cannot prove permission. |
| `untrusted_in_governance` | R-10 | A governance item is not verified or is marked untrusted_content. |
| `untrusted_content_unmarked` | R-10 | The item is in a slot whose published injection_risk default is untrusted_content (evidence.knowledge, evidence.tool_results, interaction.memory, interaction.history or interaction.query) but is not marked untrusted_content, and no MCP server the route verified produced it (R-10, R-15). |
| `protected_tier_changed` | R-16 | The item sets a tier below protected in a slot whose default tier is protected. In a slot only the route raised, an item may lower its own tier. |
| `tier_upgrade_not_allowed` | R-16 | The item claims a tier above its slot's effective tier. Only the route's versioned policy can raise a tier; a producer cannot protect its own items. |
| `duplicate_variant_id` | R-18 | Variant IDs repeat, or a variant reuses its parent item's ID. |
| `revoked` | R-9 | revoked_by is set. The item was contradicted or withdrawn. |
| `expired` | R-9 | expires is at or before assembly_time. freshness describes when content was true; a past freshness is not itself expiration. |
| `future_freshness` | R-2 | freshness is later than assembly_time by more than the route's clock_skew_seconds (default 0), compared at full precision. |
| `stale_state` | R-8 | A state item was observed longer ago than its slot's max_age_seconds. State must be current at assembly time. |
| `source_invalid` | R-3 | The item's source does not start with its slot's source_prefix. For memory, this is how the source turn is identified (R-9). |
| `out_of_scope` | R-2 | A scope key the item carries has a value other than the request's, or the request lacks that key, or the item lacks a key its slot's required_scope lists. A missing key is never a wildcard. |
| `below_threshold` | R-13 | The rerank score is under its slot's min_relevance, or the item has no score in a slot that sets one. A score equal to the threshold passes. An evidence.knowledge item always needs a score, so one without it is missing_field:relevance instead (R-13). |
| `not_eligible` | R-3 | The item was observed longer ago than its slot's max_age_seconds, in a slot other than a state slot, where the code is stale_state. The slot-level eligibility rules are the complete predicate (R-3); no other rule excludes an item this way. |
| `slot_unplaced` | R-20 | The profile has no placement for the item's slot, and the item is not protected. A protected item in an unplaced slot is never excluded; assembly refuses with protected_slot_unplaced. A profile that does not place instructions and query, or the output contract on a parser route, is rejected with its snapshot before assembly. |
| `conflict_deferred` | R-11 | The item is a peer instruction with conflict_policy defers, and the one peer in its declared conflict group that governs prevailed. A protected item is never excluded this way; its group escalates. |
| `conflict_lost` | R-11 | Route fact policy chose another member of the item's declared fact conflict group, by authenticated producer precedence or an allowed freshness tie-break. A protected item is never excluded this way; its group escalates. |
| `superseded` | R-25 | The route asked this slot to supersede by source, and the same producer sent a later observation with the same source. superseded_by names the item kept. |
| `duplicate_content` | R-24 | The item's body duplicates a kept item's: either the route asked this slot for exact deduplication and the bodies match once whitespace is collapsed (R-24), or a retriever dropped it as a near-duplicate and reported it at stage producer (R-13). duplicate_of names the item kept. |
| `source_diversity_cap` | R-26 | The route caps this slot at max_per_source items per producer and source, and higher-ranked or exempt items from the same source filled every place. |
| `over_budget` | R-16 | The item was omitted to fit the rendered budget, its own token_budget or its slot's max_tokens, in tier order and by the route's fitting policy. |

### Checking your output

- Validate each item against schema/context_item.schema.json and each batch against schema/producer_batch.schema.json with a JSON Schema 2020-12 validator that asserts `format`. The date-time `pattern` pins the shape but not the calendar, so a validator that leaves `format: date-time` unasserted accepts `2026-02-30`.
- The Producers page's item and batch linter runs the site's local checks in the browser, and so do `checkItem` and `checkProducerBatch` in https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract.js. They judge structure and the rules an item shows on its own. They cannot authenticate producers or apply the route, so producer kinds and their slots, the capability grant, the verified flag, scope, `max_age_seconds`, `min_relevance`, `source_prefix`, placement and ids across a snapshot go unchecked. Passing them is not admission.
- Admission happens in an assembler. To see it, freeze a snapshot that holds your batch and run it through one of the implementations (https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/llms-assemblers.txt): the trace's `excluded` rows say what happened to each item, and `defaults_filled` which fields the assembler filled.

- Spec, sections 2 to 4: https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/spec.html
- Requirements: https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/SPEC.md
- Item schema: https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/context_item.schema.json
- Producer-batch schema: https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/producer_batch.schema.json
- Route-policy schema, where producers, slot rules and fact precedence live: https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/schema/route_policy.schema.json
- Slot defaults: https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/contract/slot-defaults.json

- The whole contract in one file: https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/llms-full.txt

## Assemblers (llms-assemblers.txt)

> How to use a Context Window Architecture (CWA) assembler, or build one: the component that turns a frozen snapshot into a rendered payload and a trace. Three implementations exist, in Python, TypeScript and Go, built independently from the published contract, and none is released. Rules are cited by their permanent number (R-n) and are normative on the Spec page, https://contextwindowarchitecture.io/spec.html; conformance/README.md is normative wherever they leave an ordering, tie-break, boundary or algorithm step open (R-21). Its tables of refusal codes, requirement scope and implementations are generated from the contract and the imported conformance reports by the website build.

### What an assembler does

An assembler takes one snapshot, valid against schema/snapshot.schema.json: `assembly_time`, `scope`, `budget`, `profile`, `route_policy`, `tokenizer`, `renderer`, `batches` (each `{ producer: { id, kind }, items, excluded }`), `conflicts`, and, when the route admits tools, the capability grant `capabilities`. The application builds it: it runs the producers, authenticates each one, reads the clock once and freezes everything that can affect the payload (R-23). Assembly reads nothing else: no model calls (R-18), no network, no files, no ambient clock.

Every call ends in exactly one of these:

- Assembled: the payload bytes and a trace with `refused: { bool: false, reason: null }` and `result: { input_tokens, hash }`, where `hash` is the lowercase SHA-256 of the exact payload bytes (R-21).
- Refused: no payload, and a trace with `refused.bool: true`, a reason code, `result: null`, `included: []` and `compressed: []`, keeping every exclusion, conflict record and filled default recorded before the refusal (R-17). Refusals are outcomes of valid snapshots.
- Rejected: the snapshot fails its schemas or a snapshot check, so there is no payload and no trace (R-17). No reason code names a rejection; the implementation lists the problems in its own words.
- Stopped: the application supplied a tokenizer under a published tokenizer's ID, or a renderer under a published renderer's ID. There is no payload and no trace (R-16).
- Unsupported: the snapshot names a tokenizer or renderer the implementation does not provide. That is no problem with the snapshot, so it is not a rejection, and there is no payload and no trace.

Identical snapshots give identical payload bytes and hash, or the same refusal, in any process, locale or language (R-23). Only `trace_id`, `timings` and the free-text `recovery.detail` may differ between runs.

### The pipeline

The order every implementation follows, from conformance/README.md:

1. Validate. Check the snapshot against its schemas, I-JSON (no unpaired surrogates, every number a finite double) and the Snapshot checks: one batch per producer, conflict groups that name real candidates or producer exclusions with at most one group per item, producer exclusions whose `duplicate_of` or `superseded_by` names a candidate in the same batch, and a profile whose `spec` is `cwa/draft`, whose route and route-policy version match the route policy's, that places the required slots, and that the renderer can realize. Reject on any failure (R-17).
2. Admit. Check every candidate, filling and tracing the policy defaults it omits (R-3), and exclude a failure with the earliest applicable code in contract/reasons.json order (R-21). Merge the producers' own exclusion rows into the trace (R-9). Placement is the last admission check (R-20).
3. Resolve the declared conflict groups, and only those: instruction groups by authority and the peers' `conflict_policy`, fact groups by the route's precedence of authenticated producers, escalating where neither decides (R-6, R-11).
4. Supersede stale observations in the slots that set `supersede: "source"` (R-25).
5. Deduplicate exact bodies in the slots that set `dedupe: "exact"` (R-24).
6. Cap each producer and source at `max_per_source` in the slots that set it (R-26).
7. Check the refusals and fit. Refuse for a missing required slot, an unplaced protected item, an unresolved conflict or protected content that cannot fit, in that order; then enforce item caps, slot caps and budget pressure in tier order with slot floors, and refuse after fitting when a floor withheld the fit or too little evidence is left (R-4, R-12, R-16, R-17, R-20).
8. Render with the snapshot's renderer, count with its tokenizer, and hash the payload bytes.
9. Trace: every decision above, in the array orders conformance/README.md fixes (R-21, R-22).

Refusal codes, in the order the first that holds is recorded (contract/reasons.json):

| Code | Rule | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `required_slot_missing` | R-4 | governance.instructions or interaction.query, or governance.output_contract on a parser route, has no admitted item. |
| `protected_slot_unplaced` | R-20 | An admitted protected item's slot has no placement in the profile. The profile must not omit protected content, so the assembler refuses rather than drop it. |
| `conflict_unresolved` | R-11 | A declared conflict group has no unique supported resolution, and route policy says to refuse or request context. The trace records recovery.action request_context when every such group asked for context. |
| `protected_content_over_budget` | R-17 | The payload rendered from protected content alone does not fit budget.input, charged with any margin_percent, or protected items exceed their slot's max_tokens, or a protected item exceeds its own token_budget. The assembler refuses rather than truncating. |
| `slot_floor_over_budget` | R-17 | The payload does not fit budget.input without shedding a slot below the route's min_tokens. The assembler refuses rather than break the floor. |
| `evidence_required` | R-12 | The route requires evidence and too little survived admission and fitting. The trace records recovery.action. |

### The conformance claim

A conformant assembler meets every MUST an assembler can meet by itself, provides every tokenizer and renderer that conformance/README.md requires, and can emit its trace as JSON with the fields R-21 lists (spec §1). Because a model accepts any payload, a wrong decision fails silently, so the claim rests on evidence: a conformance report, valid against schema/conformance_report.schema.json, showing that the assembler passes every published case and rejects every published rejection. It may skip only a case that uses an optional tokenizer or renderer it does not provide; today all four published components are required, so it may skip none. Schema validation alone is not conformance (R-21).

A case passes when the payload matches `expected.payload.txt` byte for byte, or there is no payload where that file is absent, and the trace matches `expected.trace.json` field for field once `trace_id`, `timings` and `recovery.detail` are removed. Array order in the trace is part of the expectation. A rejection case passes when the snapshot is rejected before assembly, with no payload and no trace.

### Requirement scope

What an assembler can check of each requirement (contract/assembler-scope.json). Assembler rows are fully testable in assembly. Boundary rows are checked where the snapshot and its items are handed over, and the rest of the obligation sits with producers or the application. Application rows cannot be observed during assembly.

| Rule | Summary | Scope | What an assembler checks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-1 | One slot and one authority role per item | assembler | Admission checks each item's slot and authority. |
| R-2 | Required fields and canonical JSON shape | assembler | Schema validation with format checking; timestamps compared at full precision. |
| R-3 | Declared policy defaults, filled and traced | assembler | Fills slot defaults and versioned route overrides, records defaults_filled, and applies the four slot-level eligibility rules as the complete predicate. |
| R-4 | Slots that are never omitted | boundary | Refuses with required_slot_missing. Declaring parser: true on every route whose response a parser consumes is the application's. |
| R-5 | Rule zero: enforce outside the model | application | Application guards enforce invariants. Nothing observable in assembly can prove it. |
| R-6 | Separate instruction authority from factual precedence | assembler | Classifies each declared group as instruction or fact and resolves it by authority or route policy; only governing and user items are instruction peers, and trust and the injection marker never change that. |
| R-7 | No slot overrides platform roles; no authority from wording | assembler | Only governance takes the system and tool roles, the query is the only live user turn, history renders as a transcript in the order turns were said, and item bodies are escaped inside xml: wrappers; cwa-messages/v1 hands system and tools text over unescaped. |
| R-8 | State is application-written and current | boundary | Checks producer kind and state age. Writing state stays with the application. |
| R-9 | Memory lifetime and producer exclusion reporting | boundary | Excludes expired and revoked memory and merges producer exclusions. Reporting them is the producer's duty. |
| R-10 | User and fetched content is marked, never elevated, kept out of governance | boundary | Checks the marker in the five slots that require it, keeps unverified or marked items out of governance, and renders every body whole. Marking user-controlled and fetched content is the producer's duty, and delimiting material pasted into a body is the application's job. |
| R-11 | Explicit conflict groups and traceable resolution | boundary | Resolves the groups it is given. It cannot detect a conflict the application did not declare. |
| R-12 | Never answer from nothing | boundary | Refuses with evidence_required and a recovery action. Retrieving and summarizing before the snapshot is frozen, and freezing a new one for any retry, are the application's. |
| R-13 | Retrievers emit one scored item per chunk, never a blob | boundary | Gates retrieval producers to the evidence slots, requires the slot's authority, a score on every knowledge item and wherever the route sets a threshold, and that a reported near-duplicate names a candidate the producer kept. It cannot tell whether a producer merged chunks or dropped one silently. |
| R-14 | Memory producers suppress and report expired or revoked items | boundary | Re-excludes expired or revoked memory as a backstop. Suppressing and reporting them is the producer's duty. |
| R-15 | Authenticated capability admission; MCP output is evidence | boundary | Checks the authenticated emitter and capability grant. The application authenticates, and tool guards enforce calls. |
| R-16 | Account for rendered tokens; shed in tier order | boundary | Counts rendered tokens and sheds in tier order. Setting budget.input from the model's context limit, with a tokenizer that counts or estimates the model's tokens, is the application's. |
| R-17 | Refused assembly has no rendered payload | assembler | Refused assemblies have no payload, and their traces carry result: null and no included items. Invalid snapshots are rejected before assembly, with no payload and no trace. |
| R-18 | Precomputed variants; no model calls during assembly | boundary | Selects only supplied variants and never calls a model. It cannot verify a variant's fidelity. |
| R-19 | Draft profiles versus evaluated profiles | boundary | Rejects a profile written for another spec. Evaluation and promotion happen outside assembly: the Python assembler's registry hands a deployment only an evaluated profile, which no case covers. |
| R-20 | Profile version and mandatory-slot validation | boundary | Rejects a profile that doesn't place a required slot, and refuses the assembly when admitted protected content has no placement. Raising the version for every change is the application's; the Python assembler's registry pins content by digest, outside assembly and the cases. |
| R-21 | Trace JSON matches the published schema | assembler | Traces are checked against the schema and the reason registry, and must match every published case field for field. |
| R-22 | Provenance, snapshot digest and filled defaults in the trace | assembler | Emits source_version, eligibility, excluded slots, snapshot_digest and defaults_filled, and stage timings when the caller lends a clock. |
| R-23 | Determinism includes the clock and policy snapshot | boundary | Snapshot replay across processes, hash seeds, time zones and locales, with ordering, blank strings, timestamps and the digest pinned for every language. Making every external read and model call before the snapshot is frozen is the application's. |
| R-24 | Route-requested exact deduplication | assembler | Excludes exact duplicate bodies in the slots a route opts in, after conflicts, keeping protected and grouped items. |
| R-25 | Route-requested supersession of stale observations | assembler | Keeps only the latest observation per producer and source in the slots a route opts in, after conflicts, keeping protected and grouped items. |
| R-26 | Route-requested source diversity | assembler | Keeps at most max_per_source items per producer and source in the slots a route opts in, after dedupe, keeping protected and grouped items. |

### Tokenizers and renderers

Every implementation provides these four, exactly as conformance/README.md defines them, and every published case uses them:

- `fixture-whitespace/v1` counts maximal runs of characters outside the ECMAScript whitespace and line-terminator set. It is a test fixture, not a model tokenizer.
- `estimate-utf8/v1` counts `(UTF-8 bytes + 3)` divided by 4, discarding the remainder: a portable estimate for a model with no local tokenizer, to pair with a `budget.margin_percent` that covers its error.
- `fixture-xml/v1` renders each placed item as `<{tag} id="{id}">`, its escaped body on a line of its own, then `</{tag}>`, in placement order and by id within a placement, except history turns, which go in the order they were said: by freshness, then id (R-7). It supports only `xml:` wraps.
- `cwa-messages/v1` renders a message request, the RFC 8785 serialization of `{ system, tools, messages }`: governance placed with wrap `system` or `tools` becomes those entries, and every `xml:` placement goes into exactly one user message, rendered as `fixture-xml/v1` renders it, with prior turns marked by `speaker` as part of the transcript (R-7). The query is the only live user turn.

The payload *fits* when its count, times `(100 + margin_percent) / 100` rounded up in integer arithmetic, is at most `budget.input`; only that test takes the margin, and caps, floors and traced counts stay unscaled (R-16). An application may count with a tokenizer of its own under an ID no published tokenizer uses; an assembler stops before assembly on an application tokenizer or renderer that takes a published ID (R-16).

### Portability traps

Each is a place where languages disagree. Most have a published case written to catch them, named in parentheses with the README section that settles them; the last two no case can reach, so each implementation tests them itself.

- Strings sort by UTF-16 code units, with a prefix first. Python, Go and Rust compare code points by default, which differs beyond U+FFFF (Ordering; `ordering-astral-ids`).
- "Blank" and the whitespace tokenizer use the ECMAScript whitespace set, spelled out. Python's `\s` and `\S` differ at U+001C to U+001F and U+FEFF (Blank strings; `admission-reasons`).
- The schemas' patterns need ECMAScript regex semantics: `\uXXXX` escapes and the `(?![\s\S])` end anchor. RE2-style engines, such as Go's `regexp`, reject both.
- Assert `format: date-time`: the pattern pins the shape but not the calendar, and `admission-reasons` holds `2026-02-30` as `invalid_structure`. Compare instants at full precision, with a fraction of any length and no leap seconds (Timestamps).
- Read every number as the nearest IEEE 754 double before comparing it, so integers beyond 2^53 may tie, and reject a number outside the double range rather than crash (Numbers; `threshold-beyond-2-53`, rejection `number-out-of-range`).
- Reject an unpaired surrogate from the raw text. Some JSON parsers, Go's `encoding/json` among them, silently replace it with U+FFFD (rejection `unpaired-surrogate`).
- Serialize with RFC 8785, ECMAScript number formatting included, for the snapshot digest, the order of rows sharing an id, and the `cwa-messages/v1` payload (Snapshot digest).
- Compare deduplication keys code unit for code unit: no Unicode normalization and no case folding (Deduplication; `dedupe-exact`).
- Every reduction under budget pressure is its own fit test over the whole rendered payload, and an implementation may reach the same decisions faster but never different ones (Fitting).
- Look up tokenizer, renderer and producer IDs as own keys only: a schema-valid snapshot can name `toString` or `__proto__`.
- Sort every output by its stated keys; never iterate a hash map into output.

### Using an implementation

None is released, so work from a checkout. The table names the commit each imported report came from, with the tags on it when it was imported, and counts the report against the published cases as they are now: a case published or changed since the run does not count as passing (conformance/README.md, Reporting results).

| Language | Package | Repository | Commit | Published cases and rejections | Contract vendored at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Python | `contextwindowarchitecture-assembler` 0.0.1 | https://github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/assembler-python | `49b321e` (draft-release) | 81 of 83 pass; 1 changed since its run | website `d229b74` |
| TypeScript | `@contextwindowarchitecture/assembler` 0.0.1 | https://github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/assembler-typescript | `5e1223f` (draft-release) | 81 of 83 pass; 1 changed since its run | website `d229b74` |
| Go | `github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/assembler-go` 0.1.0 | https://github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/assembler-go | `001dadd` (draft-release) | 81 of 83 pass; 1 changed since its run | website `d229b74` |

Python, module `cwa` (Python 3.11 or newer; `uv sync` in the checkout):

```python
import json
from cwa import Snapshot, SnapshotError, UnsupportedComponentError, assemble

snapshot = Snapshot.from_json(json.load(open("snapshot.json")))  # SnapshotError rejects; .problems says why
result = assemble(snapshot)  # pure: no I/O, clock or model
result.payload    # bytes, or None when refused
result.trace      # dict matching trace.schema.json
result.refused    # trace["refused"]["bool"]
snapshot.digest() # context.snapshot_digest, the replay key
```

Pass your own tokenizers as `Snapshot.from_json(document, tokenizers={tok.id: tok})`, where any object with an `id` and a `count(text)` will do. A registry in `cwa.registry` pins profiles and route policies by digest and returns only evaluated profiles in deployment mode.

TypeScript, package `@contextwindowarchitecture/assembler` (Node.js 22 or newer, ESM; `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm run build` in the checkout):

```ts
import { assemble, checkSnapshot, SnapshotRejectedError, UnsupportedComponentError } from '@contextwindowarchitecture/assembler';

const { payload, trace } = assemble(snapshot); // payload: Uint8Array, or null when refused
```

`assemble(snapshot, { tokenizers })` takes your own tokenizers keyed by their IDs; it accepts no renderer of the application's own. `checkSnapshot(snapshot)` lists a snapshot's problems without assembling.

Go, module `github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/assembler-go`, package `assembler` (Go 1.26 or newer):

```go
result, err := assembler.Assemble(snapshotJSON, assembler.Options{})
// err is a SnapshotRejectedError or UnsupportedComponentError before assembly;
// result.Payload is nil when the assembly is refused, and result.Trace holds the trace.
```

`Options.Tokenizers` takes your own tokenizers for one call; there is no option for a renderer.

All three render examples/messages-snapshot.json to examples/messages-payload.json byte for byte, a `cwa-messages/v1` request the website's tests also derive from that snapshot.

### Building a new implementation

Start from the template, https://github.com/contextwindowarchitecture/assembler-template, and follow its PORTING.md:

1. Name the port with `scripts/init_port.py`, then vendor the contract from a website checkout with `scripts/vendor_contract.py --website ../website`. It copies the schemas, contract data, cases, rejections and registry into `vendor/cwa/`, each file pinned by SHA-256 with the website commit in `vendor/cwa.lock.json`.
2. Read conformance/README.md end to end, then contract/requirements.json, then the snapshot and trace schemas, then one case, `fixture-three-slot`, with its snapshot, trace and payload side by side. The requirements say what must happen; the README says how.
3. Build test-first, in this order: strings and instants; canonical JSON and the digest; schemas and snapshot checks (every rejection case); tokenizers and renderers; admission and defaults; conflicts, supersession, deduplication and source diversity; refusals and fitting; the trace and the runner. Unit-test each README section's rules before letting its cases pass, and keep cases the port cannot pass yet in a `PENDING` set that only shrinks.
4. Run the cases through a small adapter: `python3 scripts/conformance.py --command "<adapter>" --name <package> --version <version> --language <Language>`, then `python3 scripts/check_report.py`. The adapter reads one snapshot's raw bytes on stdin and exits 0 with `{"payload": <base64 or null>, "trace": <trace>}` on stdout for an assembly or a refusal, 2 with the problems on stderr for a rejection, and 3 for a tokenizer or renderer it does not provide.
5. Commit the report with every change that alters it. The website's maintainers import it, and the Assembler page then counts, per requirement, the cases the port passes.

Build from the published contract alone, and never read another implementation's code. Two implementations that both pass every case and still disagree have found a gap in the spec, and the fix is a spec change with a case, made in the website first and vendored after.

### What an assembler does not do

The application meets the MUSTs no component can meet for it (spec §1). It enforces invariants and tool permissions outside the model (R-5, R-15), writes state (R-8), declares conflict groups (R-11), authenticates each producer and binds its identity outside the items (R-15), makes every external read, retrieval and model call before it freezes the snapshot and freezes a new one for any retry (R-12, R-23), sets `parser: true` on every route whose response a downstream parser consumes (R-4), sets `budget.input` to the model's context limit less `budget.reserved_output` (R-16), versions its profiles (R-20) and deploys only evaluated ones (R-19). It renders with a renderer the published cases cover, and declares a tokenizer that reads nothing but the text it counts and counts the model's tokens, or estimates them with a covering margin (R-16, R-23).

It hands the payload to the model with each text in the platform role its renderer assigns, text assigned none in a single user message where the query alone is the live turn, and no text of its own. The roles R-7 has the assembler assign, and the count R-16 has it make, hold for the payload the assembler renders; only this handoff makes them hold for what the model receives.
